To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The activation of soluble guanylyl cyclase by nitric oxide (NO) is dependent on the presence of thiols.
the activation of the soluble form of guanylate cyc-lase (sGC) by nitrovasodila-tors is dependent on thiols.
the degree of soluble guanylyl cyclase activation by nitrovasodila-tor-derived nitric oxide depends on the presence and concentration of thiols.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the mechanisms of the activation of guanylate …
the elucidation of the role of thiols and the mechanism of action of nitrovasodilation, and with the search for new, more effective, and less toxic nitrovasodilater compounds.
the development of new drugs that are devoid of tolerance and have a high therapeutic index.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the activation of guanylate cyclic by nitrovasodilation is not mediated by thiols, but by nitric oxide.
thiols are not essential cofactors of soluble guanylyl cyclase activation by nitrovasodilation.
nitric oxide is the ultimate mediator of all nitrovasodilation, while thiols are required for the conversion of nitric oxide into a biologically active species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the activation of soluble guanyate cyclase by nitric oxide donors is a two-step process.
the guanylate cyclases are stimulated by nitrovasodilation in a manner dependent on the availability of thiols and that this stimulation can be achieved in a manner independent of thiols.
the guanylate cyclases are activated by NO, but the activation of the enzyme is modulated by thiol compounds.
The main takeaway from our work is that
nitrosothiols are the active species in the vasorelaxation of the nitrovasodilation pathway.
the degree of guanylyl cyclase activation by NO donors is not solely dependent on the rate of NO generation, but also on the presence of thiols.
the degree of activation of soluble guanylyl cyclase by sodium nitro-prusside increases in a concentration dependent manner in the presence of thiol compounds.
